title: The Bread Code
subtitle: A sentence that means nothing to anyone else, and the night it was finally used — by the girl who didn't have one.
description: A B1 reading and listening text: a father and his teenage daughter agree on a code phrase she can text when she wants to leave somewhere, and two years later it is used for her friend instead. The English of arrangements, promises and reported speech, with comprehension, true-or-false and vocabulary exercises.
source: authored for this site from a widely shared parenting story, adapted and set in the United States
passage: My fifteen-year-old daughter and I have a code phrase. If she texts me “Have you bought the bread yet?”, I call her five minutes later, make up an emergency, and go pick her up. No questions. No lectures. On Saturday she sent it at 11:47 at night. When I got there, two girls got into the car.

We agreed on it when she turned thirteen. She had started going to birthday parties, to sleepovers, to friends' houses I had never been inside. So I told her: “If you ever want to leave somewhere and you don't know how, text me ‘have you bought the bread yet?’. I'll call, I'll invent an excuse, and I'll come get you. And I won't ask you a single thing in the car.”

Two years went by and the code was never used. I had almost forgotten about it. On Saturday she went to a classmate's birthday party on the other side of town. I dropped her off at eight. She said goodbye, and her friend Megan was already waiting for her at the gate.

At 11:47 the phone buzzed on the arm of the couch. “Have you bought the bread yet?” I stood up so fast that my wife woke up. At 11:52 I called. “Hannah, Grandma isn't feeling well. I'm coming to pick you up right now.” She answered loudly, so that anybody standing near her could hear it: “Okay, Dad. I'll be out front.”

I pulled up at 12:06. She was waiting by the gate. Next to her was Megan, arms crossed, shaking. Three guys, a good deal older than the kids at the party, were leaning against the wall and looking at my car. The two girls got into the back seat together without saying a word.
The rule was that I don't ask questions, so I didn't ask. I turned the radio down low and drove. At the first red light I looked in the rearview mirror. Hannah was holding Megan's hand.

It was Hannah who spoke first. “Dad, the code wasn't for me. There was a guy there, maybe twenty-two, and he wouldn't leave Megan alone. He wanted to take her somewhere in his car. She said no about five times. Megan doesn't have a code with her dad. She was scared to call him. She thought it would only make things worse. So I sent mine.”

I asked Megan whether she wanted to go home. She said, very quietly, “My dad doesn't know I stayed out this late. He's going to be so mad.” She slept at our house, on a mattress on the floor of Hannah's room. My wife made the two of them hot chocolate at twenty to one in the morning.

Sunday morning I drove Megan home. Her father, Mr. Carter, opened the front door looking anything but friendly — a big man, with the arms of somebody who works with his hands. He started in on her before I had even turned the engine off. I asked whether I could talk to him first, and I told him everything: the party, the men against the wall, Hannah's code. He got quieter and quieter. Then I said something I had never said to another father. “Dale, your daughter got out of there because she had a way out. If she had been afraid to call you, she would have stayed.”

He didn't answer. He looked at his daughter, who was standing by the door staring at the ground. He ran his hand over his face. He said “thank you” without looking at me, and he went inside with her and shut the door.

Sunday night my phone buzzed again. A number I didn't know. “This is Dale, Megan's dad. How does this bread thing work?” So I explained it. A sentence that sounds like nothing. You call, you invent an emergency, you go get her. And you don't ask her anything on the way. He took a while to write back. “Ours is going to be ‘have you taken the trash out yet?’. She picked it.”

My code went two years without being used. When it was finally used, it wasn't my daughter who used it. It was her friend, who didn't have one. Agree on a phrase with your kid tonight. They don't have to explain. You don't ask questions. You just go. Because sometimes they won't use it for themselves. They'll use it for somebody who has nobody to call.

vocabulary.definition: an ordinary-sounding sentence agreed in advance, which means something else to the person who hears it
to send somebody a message on a phone
to invent something that is not true
a long serious talk telling somebody what they did wrong
a night a young person spends at a friend's house
to take somebody somewhere by car and leave them there
to vibrate and make a low sound
outside, at the front of a building
to arrive somewhere in a car and stop
with each arm folded over the other, often from cold or fear
the mirror a driver uses to see the road, and the back seat, behind them
a means of leaving a situation

exercises.title: What the Code Was For
exercises.instructions: Read for the arrangement itself: what each person promised, and what each person did.

items.prompt: What does the father promise to do when the code phrase arrives?
options: Call the parents of whoever is hosting the party
Call five minutes later, invent an emergency, and go pick her up
Text back and ask her what has happened
items.explanation: The whole arrangement is three steps and one silence: he calls, he makes something up, he drives, and he asks nothing.

items.prompt: Why does the daughter never have to explain anything?
options: Because the father already knows where she is
Because asking questions is against the rule they agreed on
Because she is not allowed to talk in the car
items.explanation: “And I won't ask you a single thing in the car.” The silence is part of what makes the phrase usable.

items.prompt: How long had the code existed before Saturday night?
options: Two years, without ever being used
items.explanation: They agreed on it when she turned thirteen, and the father says he had almost forgotten about it.

items.prompt: Why does Hannah answer the phone call so loudly?
options: Because the music at the party was very loud
So that the people around her would hear that she had a reason to leave
Because she was angry with her father
items.explanation: The invented emergency only works if somebody else hears it, which is why he invents one at all.

items.prompt: Who had the code actually been used for?
options: Hannah, who wanted to come home early
Megan, who had no code with her own father
Both girls, who were bored at the party
items.explanation: “Dad, the code wasn't for me.” Hannah sent her phrase on behalf of somebody who had none.

items.prompt: Why had Megan not called her own father?
options: Her phone had no battery left
She was scared to call him and thought it would only make things worse
She did not know his number
items.explanation: The fear of the reaction is what kept her at the party — the point the narrator makes to her father the next morning.

items.prompt: What does the narrator say to Mr. Carter that he had never said to another father?
options: That his daughter should not be allowed out so late
That she got out of there because she had a way out, and would have stayed if she had been afraid to call him
That he would drive her home every weekend from now on
items.explanation: It is a third conditional: a different past (being afraid to call) would have produced a different night.

items.prompt: How does the reader know Mr. Carter changed his mind?
options: He apologizes to his daughter in front of the narrator
He texts that night to ask how the code works, and says his daughter chose their phrase
He drives to the narrator's house on Monday
items.explanation: He says almost nothing at the door; the change shows up later, as a question from an unknown number.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the story.

items.statement: The father asked the girls what had happened as soon as they got into the car.
items.explanation: False — “The rule was that I don't ask questions, so I didn't ask.” Hannah speaks first, by herself.

items.statement: Grandma really was unwell on Saturday night.
items.explanation: False — the grandmother is the invented emergency the code requires.
False — she slept on a mattress in Hannah's room, and the narrator drove her home on Sunday morning.

items.statement: Mr. Carter began criticizing his daughter before the narrator had even turned the engine off.
items.explanation: True — “He started in on her before I had even turned the engine off.”

items.statement: Megan's family chose the same phrase about bread.
items.explanation: False — theirs is “have you taken the trash out yet?”, and Megan picked it herself.

items.statement: The narrator thinks a code phrase is only useful for your own child.
items.explanation: False — the last lines say the opposite: sometimes they use it for somebody who has nobody to call.

exercises.title: Arrangements, Rides and Phones
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the right word or phrase from the text.

items.prompt: We ___ ___ a phrase that sounds completely normal to everybody else.
items.explanation: To agree on something is to decide it together; the preposition is fixed.

items.prompt: He ___ an emergency so that nobody at the party would ask her why she was leaving.
items.explanation: Invent, or make up — both appear in the text for the same act.

items.prompt: I ___ her ___ at eight and promised to come back whenever she called.
items.explanation: You drop somebody off when you leave them somewhere, and pick them up when you collect them.

items.prompt: The phone ___ on the arm of the couch at a quarter to midnight.
items.explanation: A phone on silent buzzes — it vibrates and makes a low sound.

items.prompt: He wouldn't ___ her ___ , however many times she said no.
items.explanation: To leave somebody alone is to stop bothering them.

items.prompt: She left the party because she had ___ ___ ___ ; without one she would have stayed.
items.explanation: A way out is a means of leaving a situation — the sentence the narrator says to Mr. Carter.

discussion: The rule is that the parent asks no questions. Why would a code phrase stop working without that part?
Megan was more afraid of her father's reaction than of the man at the party. What does that tell you about how the two fathers had each behaved before that night?
Would you have broken the no-questions rule in the car? Say why, or why not.
Megan chose her family's phrase herself. Why might that matter more than which phrase it is?
Write about 150 words about an arrangement you have with somebody in your family — a phrase, a signal, or a promise — and explain how it works and when it is used.
